findings.F1: The large 24-hour fall is what rebounds, whatever the hour. On the non-overlapping 24-bar grid, bars in the bottom decile of the 24-hour return (scaled by the mean absolute 24-hour move of the last 720 bars) are followed by a 24-hour return of +82.6 bp above the coin's normal drift (t 5.21, 1581 cases). The next decile gives only +19.8 bp (t 1.53). The middle and top deciles give between -4 and -26 bp, so the rebound sits in the deepest falls.
findings.F2: That rebound is much larger than the tested idea's. For the bottom two deciles of the 24-hour move, the strength is 0.102 of the coin's usual 24-hour move, against 0.031 for the settlement-fall cases. At +43 to +83 bp per case, the unusual move alone covers the 0.19 % cost of a trade.
findings.F3: The rebound after large 24-hour falls lives almost entirely in high-volatility stretches. When the 1-week hourly volatility over the 1-month volatility is above its median, it is +103.7 bp (t 6.17, 1277 cases); below the median it is -10.3 bp (t -0.74, 1278 cases).

ideas.idea: After a coin falls sharply over 24 hours, it rises over the next 24 hours, and the larger the fall against its usual 24-hour move, the larger the rise, at any hour of the day.
ideas.consequence: A trader buys deep one-day falls on any hour rather than only at settlement times, and expects a rebound several times larger per case than the settlement fall gave.
ideas.name: deep daily fall rebounds

ideas.idea: When a coin's hourly volatility over the past week is high against its past month, a sharp 24-hour fall is followed by a rise over the next 24 hours, and the larger the fall against its usual 24-hour move, the larger the rise.
ideas.consequence: A trader buys deep one-day falls when the market has turned turbulent, and refuses them in calm stretches, where they do not rebound.
ideas.name: turbulent fall rebound
